_readme: Content AISA has written to fill gaps in the published ADEK pack.
The pack's lessons refer to printed artefacts a teacher hands out — a dataset card, a
criteria card — and to diagrams that exist as images in the PDF and so did not survive
text extraction. A student reading the lesson on screen is told to 'read the three lenses
on the criteria card' with no card in front of them.
These supplements fill those specific holes. They are kept separate from the extracted
lessons, and every section is marked authored:true so it renders with a note saying it is
AISA's addition and not ADEK material. Nothing here changes a worksheet task, a mark
scheme or a framework tag — only what a student reads.
insertAfter names the heading of the published section this should follow; 'start' places
it first.
DIAGRAMS
A diagram is added where the lesson teaches something that is structural — a sequence, a
comparison, a set of named parts, a decision with several outcomes, a loop — and prose
alone leaves the student assembling the shape themselves. Not for decoration, and not to
reconstruct figures from the PDF that nobody has seen.
Five variants, chosen to fit what the lesson actually claims:
flow     a chain where each step causes the next, with the link named on the arrow
compare  two mechanisms side by side, so the difference is the thing you look at
parts    one thing made of named parts, drawn as one bar rather than a list
branch   one input sorting into several named outcomes
loop     a cycle you go round until it is good enough
Picking the wrong variant misrepresents the lesson: drawn as a chain, refining a prompt
looks like something you finish, which is the opposite of what the lesson teaches. If a
concept does not fit any of the five, add a variant rather than forcing it into one.
altText is required and is what a screen reader announces, so it must carry the same
information as the picture, not name it.

g6-bridging-w1-core.insertAfter: The model learns from its examples

section.label: How a data problem becomes an output mistake
section.heading: One flaw, traced all the way to the answer
section.altText: A chain of three boxes: a data problem leads to a wrong learned pattern, which leads to a wrong output.
section.caption: This is the chain you trace on your worksheet. Start at the data, not the answer.

nodes.label: The output is wrong
nodes.detail: it calls a pebble a date

g6-bridging-w1-core.insertAfter: Quality is not the same as quantity

section.label: Your dataset card
section.heading: What a dataset card shows you
section.intro: Your teacher gives you a card describing one dataset. Read it in this order — the flaw is never announced, you have to find it.

entries.asks: How many items are there, and what is each one a picture of?
entries.test: A small set is not automatically a bad one.

entries.asks: What is each example called? Is every label correct?
entries.test: One wrong label teaches one wrong lesson.

entries.asks: Does the set cover the real range of cases, or only some of them?
entries.test: A gap is as damaging as an error.

entries.asks: Is anything blurry, inconsistent or irrelevant?
entries.test: Noise makes the pattern harder to find.

g6-bridging-w2-core.insertAfter: Change one thing, and know why

section.label: Refining is a loop, not a line
section.heading: Judge, change one thing, judge again
section.altText: A loop: judge the output you got, change one thing about the prompt, run it again, then judge whether that change helped.
section.repeatLabel: not good enough yet — go round again
section.caption: A prompt is rarely right first time, and that is normal. **Keeping the receipts — which change, what happened — is what turns guessing into refining.**

g6-bridging-w3-core.insertAfter: A solution is data plus a model

section.label: What a solution is made of
section.heading: Data plus a model
section.altText: A bar split into two parts — the data and the model — which together produce the outcome.

parts.label: The model
parts.detail: the pattern it found in them

section.caption: Change the data and the outcome changes, even with the same model. **That is why tracing a bad outcome starts at the data**, not at the answer.

g6-bridging-w4-core.insertAfter: Why fluent is not the same as true

section.label: Why a wrong answer can sound right
section.heading: Fluent and true are decided separately
section.altText: A chain: the model predicts what usually comes next, which makes the answer read smoothly, which is why it sounds right whether or not it is true.

nodes.label: It predicts what usually comes next

section.caption: Nothing in that chain checks a fact. **Sounding right is produced by the same process whether the answer is true or false**, so it can never be your evidence.

section.label: The three parts you are designing
section.heading: A helper has three parts
section.altText: A bar split into three parts — the data it uses, the prompt that drives it, and the checks that catch mistakes — which together make a helper you can trust.

parts.label: Its prompt
parts.detail: what you ask it to do

section.caption: All three are yours to design. **A helper with no checks is not finished** — it is a helper you are hoping about.

section.label: The distinction the whole unit rests on
section.heading: Where did the rule come from?
section.altText: Two columns. In a rule-based machine a person writes the rule and the machine follows it. In a learning machine, examples go in and the machine works the rule out for itself.

left.title: Rule-based machine
steps: A person works out the rule
They write it down as steps

right.title: Learning machine
steps: The machine finds the rule in them
The machine uses what it found

section.caption: Same job, different source. Ask **who worked out the rule** — that is the question this unit keeps coming back to.

section.label: The difference you are looking for
section.heading: Two ways a system can reach an answer
section.altText: Two columns. A rule-based system takes an input, follows a rule a person wrote, and gives an output. A learning system takes labelled examples, finds a pattern itself, and uses that pattern on a new input.
section.caption: Both give an answer. The difference is **where the rule came from** — a person wrote it, or the system found it.

left.title: Rule-based system
steps: Follow the rule a person wrote

right.title: Learning system
steps: Use it on a new input

section.label: The shape of a structured prompt
section.heading: One prompt, three slots
section.altText: A single bar split into three labelled slots — Goal, Context and Format — which together make a prompt the tool can act on.

parts.label: Goal
parts.detail: What you want it to do

parts.label: Context
parts.detail: What it needs to know first

section.result: A prompt the tool can act on
section.caption: Leave a slot empty and the tool fills it with a guess of its own. **Format is the one most often left out**, and it is why an answer comes back in the wrong shape.

section.label: What to do with an output
section.heading: Three verdicts, not two
section.source: An output you have just read
section.altText: One output leads to three possible verdicts: correct, incorrect, or unclear.

branches.label: Correct
branches.detail: You checked it against something else

branches.label: Incorrect
branches.detail: You found something that is wrong

branches.label: Unclear
branches.detail: You could not check it either way

section.caption: **Unclear is a real verdict**, not a way of avoiding one. It records what you were unable to check, which is information the next person needs.

section.label: Two families, different responses
section.heading: What kind of risk is this?
section.altText: A risk splits into two families: the output being wrong, and the tool being used unsafely. Each has a different response.

branches.label: The output is wrong
branches.detail: → check it before anyone acts on it

branches.label: The use is unsafe
branches.detail: → change what goes in, or do not use it

section.caption: Naming the family tells you the response. **Checking harder does not fix a privacy problem**, and removing personal details does not make a wrong fact right.

section.label: The whole term in one line
section.heading: Four skills, one chain
section.altText: A chain of four steps: work out the system type, write a structured prompt, triage the output, then run a risk check.

edges.label: so you know what to expect
so the output is worth judging
so you know what you are risking

section.caption: Each step only makes sense because of the one before it. **Skip the first and you do not know what the tool was ever going to be able to do.**

section.label: Criteria card
section.heading: The three lenses
section.intro: Judge your solution through each lens in turn. A solution can be accurate and still fail the other two.

entries.asks: How often does it give the right or sensible answer?
entries.test: Test it with examples where you already know the correct answer, and record the score.

entries.asks: Does it actually help your user do their task?
entries.test: Check it against the real task you designed it for, not a task that happens to suit it.

entries.asks: What could go wrong, and who could be harmed?
entries.test: Check for unfair results and for any private data being exposed.

section.label: How to prove a change worked
section.heading: One change at a time, with evidence
section.altText: A loop: judge the solution against the criteria, change one thing, run it again, and judge again to see whether that change helped.
section.repeatLabel: still short of the criteria — go round again
section.caption: Same input each time, one change each time. **Change two things at once and you cannot say which one worked** — which is the evidence you are being asked for.
